query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The unusual stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of the HfNbTaTiZr alloy arises from temperature‐induced elemental segregation and nano‐precipitate formation that, through differential thermal expansion with the surrounding matrix, generate localized residual stresses. These internal stresses alter dislocation mobility, leading to highly temperature‐dependent creep, hardening during deformation, and anomalous elastic moduli responses.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy produced via rapid quenching to minimize initial segregation and ensure homogeneity.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal treatments: (a) aging at 600–800 °C to promote slight elemental segregation and nano‐precipitate formation and (b) compare with rapidly quenched homogeneous samples. Then, subject samples to high‐temperature tensile creep at 1250 °C, cold rolling with subsequent microhardness testing, and elastic modulus measurements from 293 to 1100 K.
generation.conditions: Tests include tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness evaluation following room‐temperature cold rolling, and elastic modulus measurements between 293 K and 1100 K. Aging treatments should be applied at 600–800 °C to provoke controlled microstructural changes.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale precipitates and locally segregated regions (especially involving elements like Ta, Hf, and Zr) that develop due to thermal treatment and thermal expansion mismatch.
generation.mechanism: Differential thermal expansion between the precipitate-rich (or segregated) regions and the homogeneous BCC matrix induces local residual stresses. These stresses modify the dislocation dynamics by increasing dislocation pinning and lattice friction, thereby enhancing high-temperature creep resistance, augmenting work hardening during cold deformation, and affecting the temperature dependency of the elastic moduli. Aging accelerates or refines these effects through stable nano-precipitate formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the homogeneous (rapid-quenched) baseline, samples with induced segregation/precipitation will exhibit: (1) increased high-temperature tensile creep resistance (lower steady-state creep rate at 1250 °C), (2) higher microhardness after cold rolling due to enhanced dislocation pinning, and (3) a modified elastic modulus behavior (potentially a reduced temperature sensitivity) in the 293–1100 K range.
generation.baseline: Rapid-quenched, single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy with minimal elemental segregation and precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under controlled high-temperature (≥1000 °C for creep) and moderate temperature (293–1100 K for elastic moduli) conditions. It may not apply if oxidation or other impurity-induced phenomena dominate the microstructural evolution, or if extensive phase separation beyond nano-scale occurs.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative trend is supported by prior evidence of phase segregation and related mechanical changes in similar alloys, the quantitative contributions of thermal expansion mismatch, segregation, and precipitate-induced dislocation pinning remain to be fully delineated. The interplay among these factors and their precise effects on different mechanical properties require further detailed experimental clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HfNbTaTiZr alloys: (a) one rapidly quenched to maintain a homogeneous single-phase microstructure, and (b) one subjected to an aging treatment (600–800 °C) to induce controlled elemental segregation and nano-precipitate formation. Conduct identical tests on both: tensile creep experiments at 1250 °C, cold rolling followed by microhardness measurements at room temperature, and elastic modulus tests over 293–1100 K. Use TEM and XRD to verify microstructural differences.
measurements: Elastic modulus as a function of temperature (293–1100 K)
Microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD) to quantify segregation/precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged (segregated/precipitated) samples do not exhibit statistically significant differences in tensile creep resistance, microhardness, or elastic modulus behavior relative to the homogeneous baseline—and if no corresponding microstructural differences are observed—then the hypothesis that differential thermal expansion arising from segregation/precipitation governs the alloy’s unusual mechanical response would be falsified.

In addition, some recent studies have highlighted the substantial impact of oxygen and nitrogen additions, in the range of 1 to 3 atomic % (at %) (, , ), on the mechanical properties of HEAs. For instance, Cui et al. () demonstrated that a Ti-V-Hf-Nb alloy with ~2 at % oxygen additions can reach a yield strength of 1.5 GPa, while maintaining substantial ductility. Similarly, Lei et al. () reported that by introducing 2 at % N, the tensile strength of a Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb alloy can surge by over 70%. These interstitials are often incorporated at trace levels during processing RHEAs and can accumulate further in service. However, a notable knowledge gap remains, especially regarding the behavior of these oxygen/nitrogen interstitials during high-temperature aging. cited_evidence.text: Overall, this comprehensive study provides evidence for the unique elastic and plastic deformation behavior of the single BCC solid-solution phase refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using in situ neutron experiments coupled with theoretical calculations. The results of the ND and characterization of the microstructure show the excellent BCC single-phase stability up to 900°C. Furthermore, the present alloy has the high yield strength and excellent plasticity at RT and softening resistance at elevated temperatures. The lattice strain evolution results show the distinctive elastic deformation behavior as an elastic isotropy at RT and less temperature dependency in the elastic anisotropic deformation behavior than conventional metallic materials at elevated temperatures. The single-crystal elastic moduli are obtained from the in situ ND data coupled with the Kroner model approach, showing excellent agreement with the experimental values determined from RUS measurements and first-principles calculations. AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
